title: Short Stuff: Milk Wars
summary: Short Stuff episode on the Chicago Milk War of the 1930s. Josh and Chuck explain that the conflict is loosely associated with Al Capone but was really run by his successors while he was in federal prison. The Chicago mob moved into the milk business, partly because Prohibition's repeal threatened bootlegging profits, and used violence and intimidation against the milk wagon drivers union led by Steve Sumner. The mob bought Meadow Gold Dairies to hire non-union workers and undercut fixed milk prices. Dairy industry players fought back, including bombing the mob's dairy. The hosts then digress into movie talk (Johnny Dangerously, Top Secret, After Hours) and cereal naming jokes. They describe a 1939 antitrust case that ended in an agreement requiring independent producers, distributors, and stores to be allowed to compete, and say the whole affair ended around 1940.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the Short Stuff episode with banter about Dave and Obi-Wan jokes, and Chuck says they lack coverage of the Chicago mob era.

segments.title: Setting up the Chicago Milk War
segments.summary: Josh explains the milk war takes place in 1933 and lasted through the 1930s. It is associated with Al Capone, but his successors ran it while he was in federal prison, so he had little direct involvement.

segments.title: Why the mob moved into milk
segments.summary: Chuck explains Capone was jailed for tax evasion, first in Atlanta and then Alcatraz. The mob diversified from bootlegging and speakeasies as Prohibition repeal approached, choosing milk because it was lightly regulated. They already ran an artichoke racket and cheese and whiskey rackets.

segments.title: Mob violence against the milk union
segments.summary: Josh says the mob used violence and intimidation, first targeting the office of Steve Sumner, leader of Milk Wagon Drivers Union Local 753. The existing dairy alliance was already uneasy and fixing prices, and the mob's arrival caused chaos.

segments.title: Mob buys a dairy and offers protection
segments.summary: Milk prices were fixed and drivers were unionized. The Chicago mob bought Meadow Gold Dairies to hire non-union workers and undercut prices. Murray the Camel Humphries approached Sumner with a deal: lay low and the mob would offer protection.

segments.title: Dairy industry fights back
segments.summary: Josh says that after the mob threatened to break heads, people in the dairy industry bombed the mob's dairy. Chuck jokes about the movie Johnny Dangerously as a comparison.

segments.title: Break and movie tangent
segments.summary: Mid-episode break. The hosts talk about Johnny Dangerously, Top Secret, Griffin Dunne, and After Hours. This is a tangent rather than a sponsor read.

segments.title: Competing groups in the milk trade
segments.summary: Josh explains the groups in the milk business: farmers who produce milk, milk dealers' association that fixed prices, stores that sold cheaper milk, and union delivery companies. Each competed fiercely with the others while the public resisted higher prices.

segments.title: Cereal naming tangent and band names
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh joke about whether the mob called cereal granola, and recall the Kellogg's episode. They also mention union names such as the Pure Milk Association and Milk Wagon Drivers Union.

segments.title: 1939 antitrust case and resolution
segments.summary: Chuck describes a 1939 antitrust case where a district court threw out the suit, which was later reinstated by the Supreme Court. The DOJ reached an agreement that barred price fixing and allowed independent producers, distributors and stores to compete. Josh notes Sumner's bafflement and says the affair ended around 1940.

segments.title: Sign-off and sponsor line
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck close the episode, and the iHeartRadio podcast credit is read.
